data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is primarily driven by the delayed release of sensible heat stored in high thermal mass urban materials (asphalt, concrete), and the cross-city gap scales with the areal fraction of impervious surfaces and building density, which increase daytime heat storage.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If rural thermal mass (e.g., dry bare rock or desert) equals or exceeds urban thermal mass, the storage-release mechanism fails to generate a significant nocturnal UHI.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If high regional wind speeds thoroughly mix the urban canopy layer with rural air, the local thermal storage release is advected away, neutralizing the gap.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"During the day, urban materials with high heat capacity and thermal mass absorb incoming solar radiation. After sunset, as the atmospheric boundary layer stabilizes, these materials release stored sensible heat via longwave radiation and conduction, slowing the urban cooling rate relative to the countryside. The magnitude of this effect is larger in cities with greater impervious surface area and built density because they store more daytime heat.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
